facets.name: the human's observations about this instance
facets.source: the human, in the session that crashed (and in this one)

instances.text: (5,10) is the best starting point. Have you use it to trim? It should connect to a 8-cell and a 12-cell blocks, because of 9 and 13 reading.
instances.derivation: F-singleton-demand makes (5,10) the unique 1x1 state at that end of the board; F-ring puts d = 1 on (5,9) and (6,10); F-area then gives |9-1| = 8 and |13-1| = 12
instances.caveat: the chain uses d(6,10) = 1, i.e. (6,10) is NOT a capitol.  The branch where it IS gives 9 and 13 instead -- not refuted, weaker.

instances.text: the 9 one-cell states (the '9 + 2' reading): the frame is a few known sizes of small state + several big states + filler
instances.status: WITHDRAWN -- the supporting arithmetic does not hold
instances.note: the crashed session read it as '32 of the 121 cells are already pinned into big states'.  It is a CLAIM ABOUT THE SHAPE OF THE SOLUTION, not a constraint the engine can check.
why_withdrawn: F-area pins 12 CELLS, not 32 (10 of them with min_area >= 4, 2 with min_area = 2) -- the '32' was never measured
and 'min_area >= 4' is a LOWER bound, which points the OPPOSITE way from 'is a singleton'.  A lower bound of 4 cannot imply size 1.
so 'F-area already pins 32 cells into states of area >= 4.  The claim is that NINE of them are singletons' never had a valid inference behind it
instances.what_is_left: the d=1 demands are strong on their OWN -- a d=1 cell is one cost-1 step from a 1x1 state, and a 1x1 state IS a capitol (PLAN D64).  F-singleton-demand and F-ball carry that.  The number '9' is not derived from F-area and must not be carried as if it were.
instances.the_load_bearing_reading: the thing that does carry weight is the TIGHT reading of 13 = 12 + 1 and 61 = 12*5 + 1 (facet F-inferred, I7), not the count '9'.

facets.name: what the published readings force about the state sizes
facets.source: derived in tools/infer_sizes_11x11.py from the readings alone

instances.rule: I1 (adjacency bound): for adjacent cells x,y, |d(x) - d(y)| <= min(size_x, size_y)
instances.consequence: each published cell inherits a LOWER BOUND on its state's size from every published neighbour
instances.worked_example: (10,8)=77 and (10,9)=61 are adjacent, so both states have at least 16 cells

instances.rule: I2 (path decomposition): a reading v is k steps inside the state (cost size each) plus ONE crossing of cost r = min(size, next size)
instances.consequence: v = k*size + r with 1 <= r <= size, or v = k*size when the path ends on the state's OWN capitol (then the area is ODD)

the_two_load_bearing_cases.r = 1: the crossing costs 1 -> the next state has ONE cell -> it is a SINGLETON CAPITOL (the human's pattern: 61 = 12*5+1, 13 = 12+1)
the_two_load_bearing_cases.r = 0: the path ends inside the state -> that state has a capitol -> its area is ODD (D43)

instances.consequence: the 12-cell state does NOT CONTAIN (10,9): if it did, the step (10,8)->(10,9) would cost at most 12 and d(10,8) <= 12 + 61 = 73 < 77.  So (10,9)'s own state has >= 16 cells and its path CROSSES INTO the 12-cell state (crossing cost min(size_9, 12) = 12).
instances.correction: an earlier note here said the reading '61 = 12*5 + 1' was refuted.  That was WRONG: the reading survives, provided the five 12-cost steps are one CROSSING plus four inside the 12-cell state.  The human's arithmetic is right; only the anchor was wrong (the 12 belongs to the state entered, not to the state left).

instances.rule: I4 (the singleton-exit sizes): with the bound from I3 applied, the readings admit only these state sizes
instances.consequence: the human's '51 implies a LARGE shape in the upper middle' is sizes 25 or 50; the '61' cell's state is 20, 30 or 60 -- NOT 12

instances.rule: I5 (the tight edge of the 77): if the tight neighbour of (10,8) is (10,9), the crossing costs 77 - 61 = 16 = min(size_8, size_9)
instances.consequence: exactly one of the two states has 16 cells, and since the (10,9) state's singleton-exit sizes are 20/30/60, it is the (10,8) state that has 16 cells
instances.status: PROVISIONAL (it rests on the 'travel right' hypothesis)

instances.rule: I6 (the exit singleton is hidden): the singleton that ends the (10,9) path is NOT the revealed capitol (10,5)
instances.why: the exit cell is at within-state distance k from (10,9), and k <= 3 for every candidate size; (10,5) is at Manhattan 4, and the only 3-step path from (10,9) to a neighbour of (10,5) runs through (10,8), which belongs to the 16-cell state
instances.consequence: there is a HIDDEN 1-cell capitol within Manhattan 4 of (10,9)

instances.rule: I7 (where the 12-cell state is): 13 = 12 + 1 and 61 = 12*5 + 1 are the SAME chain
the_chain: the (5,10) singleton is a 1-cell state, so its ring (4,10), (5,9), (6,10) all have d = 1
d(6,10) = 1 for FREE: one step into a 1-cell state costs exactly 1, whatever the size of (6,10)'s own state
d(7,10) = 13 = 12 + 1  =>  the step (7,10)->(6,10) costs 12 =>  a 12-cell state touches (7,10) and (6,10)
d(10,9) = 61 = 12*5 + 1  =>  the path is (10,9) --crossing--> the 12-cell state --4 steps inside--> (6,10) --1--> (5,10)
the Manhattan distance (10,9)->(6,10) is exactly 5 and (6,10)->(5,10) is 1, so the whole path is MONOTONE: 6 steps for a Manhattan distance of 6.  That is a tight fit and it is why the reading works.
instances.consequence: the 12-cell state contains (6,10), (7,10) and an ENTRY cell (9,9) or (10,10) 4 steps from (6,10) inside the state.  It does NOT contain (10,8) or (10,9) (both have size >= 16).
instances.the_condition: the tight neighbour of (7,10) is assumed to be (6,10); the alternatives (8,10) and (7,9) are unpublished.  So this is the READING, not a theorem.  What IS a theorem: d(6,10) = 1.
instances.measured: 1044 twelve-cell states contain both (6,10) and (7,10); 783 of them hold no revealed capitol

instances.status: PROVISIONAL (it follows from I7; it is not published)

instances.rule: I9 (the 51 chain): 51 = 50 + 1 puts a 50-cell state around (3,3), and it points at ONE hidden singleton that serves three readings
the_chain: d(2,5) = 1 and d(3,6) = 1  =>  each is adjacent to a 1-cell state
(3,5) and (2,6) are adjacent to BOTH (2,5) and (3,6), so ONE singleton can serve both
d(3,3) = 51 = 50 + 1  =>  (3,3) is one step (cost 50) from a cell that is adjacent to a 1-cell state
so: the singleton at (3,5) [or (2,6)], and a 50-cell state containing (3,3) and (3,4) -- then (3,4) -> (3,5) costs min(50, 1) = 1
instances.why_it_matters: this is the human's 'the 51 is near the two 1 readings, so there is a large shape in the upper middle' -- and it identifies WHICH large shape and WHICH singleton
instances.status: PROVISIONAL (the tight-neighbour conditions are not published)

instances.rule: I10 (the conservation clash): the 50-cell state and the 45-cell state cannot both exist
instances.arithmetic: 50 (upper middle, from 51 = 50 + 1) + 45 (around (8,8), from 45 = 45 + 0) + 16 + 12 + 8 + 1 = 132 > 121 = the whole board
instances.consequence: at most ONE of them.  The two readings 51 and 45 are consistent with each other only through this: one of them is a large state and the other is not.

instances.rule: I12 (the corner chain, run): the surviving corner triples
instances.the_chain: d(6,10)=1 is free; d(7,10)=13=12+1 puts a 12-cell state on (7,10) and (6,10); d(10,9)=61=12*5+1 crosses INTO that state and walks 4 steps to (6,10) then exits to the (5,10) singleton; |77-61|=16 puts both (10,8) and (10,9) in a 16-cell state; d(6,9)=9=8+1 forces size(6,9)=8 exactly.
instances.measured: the chain cuts the blind search from 347,802 pairs to 149 12-cell + 630 8-cell + 7,534 16-cell candidates
instances.the_two_branches: the '8' in 9 = 8 + 1 has TWO carriers -- (6,9)'s own state, or the state holding (5,9) -- because both (5,9) and (6,10) are d=1 neighbours of (6,9).  L2/L3 cannot separate them, so both are enumerated: 483 candidates carry it at (6,9), 399 at (5,9), 252 at both.
instances.the_surviving_split: of the triples that survive every published reading inside them, the overwhelming majority have the 8 carried by (5,9), and only a small minority by (6,9).  The 12-cell state's 12 cells are FIXED in every survivor.
instances.the_sampling_bias_trap: an earlier version of this note said the 12-cell state's twelve cells were FIXED.  That was sampling bias: the stored samples are the FIRST 60 survivors, all from one branch.  Measured over all 58,765, only (6,10) and (7,10) are certain, and the 8-cell state's core is five cells ((2,9) (3,9) (4,9) (4,10) (5,9)).
instances.status: PROVEN (the chain and the split); PROVISIONAL (the tight-edge choices and the tails of the 16-cell state)

instances.why: measured: a triple whose 8-cell state reaches (10,10) gives a local d(10,9) of 53, not 61 -- the 8-cell state offers a cheaper route than the 12-cell one.  L1 tightness bites a cell other than the one being solved.

(8,8) lands inside the 12-cell state in 60 of 60 samples; the local field gives 49 against a published 45 (an upper bound, so no contradiction, but the path is not the 4-step one).  The only decomposition that works is 45 = 12*3 + 9: three steps inside the 12-cell state, then a crossing of cost 9 into a NINE-cell state.
instances.consequence: (8,8) sits exactly 3 steps from (6,10) inside the 12-cell state, and a 9-cell state exists next to it

instances.rule: I11 (how many singletons the readings force)
instances.measured: the five d=1 cells ((2,5), (3,6), (4,10), (5,9) and the derived (6,10)) are covered by TWO singletons: (5,10) covers (4,10), (5,9), (6,10); (3,5) [or (2,6)] covers (2,5) and (3,6) -- and the same (3,5) singleton is the one I9 needs for 51 = 50 + 1
instances.status: PROVEN for the cover; the CHOSEN positions are PROVISIONAL

facets.name: readings that were guessed, and then refuted by the published numbers
facets.source: the human's corner hypothesis, re-checked here

instances.why_it_is_false: (10,8) = 77 and (10,9) = 61 are ADJACENT, and for adjacent cells |d(x) - d(y)| <= min(size_x, size_y), so both states have at least 16 cells.  A 12-cell state at (10,9) would also give d(10,8) <= 12 + 61 = 73 < 77.
instances.what_survives: the ARITHMETIC of the human's reading survives exactly: 61 = 12*5 + 1 and 13 = 12 + 1 use the SAME 12-cell state and the SAME singleton at (5,10).  Only the anchor moves: the 12-cell state is the one the path CROSSES INTO, and it holds (6,10) and (7,10).  See I7.
instances.status: WITHDRAWN as stated; the reading itself is PROVISIONAL (I7)

instances.rule: R3: 'the 16-cell block at (10,8)' -- i.e. that a 16-cell state holds (10,8) and that the crossing to (10,9) costs 16
instances.status: PROVISIONAL, not withdrawn: the LOWER BOUND min >= 16 is proven (I3), and the equality needs the tight edge of the 77 to be (10,9) (I5).  The enumeration found 25,749 sixteen-cell states containing (10,8), 7,735 of them legal under the per-block filters -- but 0 of them fit beside the 12-block the trim had picked, and that 12-block was in the wrong place (I7).

facets.name: rules that were stated and then refuted
facets.source: the crashed session's last turn, and re-checked here

instances.rule: R1: a capitol at s => every published neighbour of s has d <= 1
instances.claimed_consequence: the hidden-capitol pool shrinks from 88 cells to 15, and no cover of size <= 5 exists
instances.why_it_is_false: the step from x to an adjacent capitol c costs min(size_x, size_c), and BOTH sizes can be large.  So d(x) <= min(size_x, size_c), which is NOT <= 1.  A cell with d = 8 can sit next to a capitol of a 12-cell state.
instances.consequence: the 15-cell pool and the '>5 hidden capitols' number are VOID. Do not use them.  (The crashed session retracted this itself in its last thinking, one turn before it degenerated.)
